extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of public relations, public affairs officers (military) and nonprofit communications professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for practicing public relations in military and nonprofit organizations, including professionalization, audience-centered messaging, fundraising principles, cause-marketing, and media relations practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organized
rubrics_metrics.description: The organization has a charter, regular meetings, officers, rules, or other indicators of relative permanence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonprofit organizations are institutionally separate from government, even if they receive government funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not-for-profit
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonprofit organizations can make a profit and reinvest it in the agency, but cannot distribute profits to those who manage or direct it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-governing
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonprofit organizations govern themselves and their activities, have their own boards of directors and provide opportunities for citizen involvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be some voluntary participation in the management of the organization, meaning that there is some aspect of charitable contribution involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of PR — define/brand to build top-of-mind awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Define or “brand” the organization to build “top-of-mind” awareness, gain acceptance of its mission, and protect its reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of PR — develop channels of communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop channels of communication with target audiences, including those the organization serves and those that can impact the nonprofit’s performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of PR — create/maintain favorable climate for fund-raising
rubrics_metrics.description: Create and maintain a favorable climate for fund-raising and coordinate communication strategies for fund-raising campaigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Exhibit 18.1 for detailed fund-raising principles and campaign operation guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of PR — support public policy favorable to mission
rubrics_metrics.description: Support the development and maintenance of public policy that is favorable to the organization’s mission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of PR — recruit and motivate key constituents
rubrics_metrics.description: Recruit and motivate key organizational constituents (such as employees, volunteers, and trustees) to support the organization’s mission, goals, and objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fund-raising — Preparation: five essentials of a successful campaign
rubrics_metrics.description: The five essentials of a successful campaign are a strong case, effective leadership, conscientious workers, prospects willing and able to give, and sufficient funds to finance the campaign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fund-raising — Preparation: coordinate committee and publicity work
rubrics_metrics.description: Committee work and publicity work should be coordinated and spelled out in detail in advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fund-raising — Preparation: estimate campaign cost in advance
rubrics_metrics.description: The cost of a campaign, within reasonable limits, should be estimated in advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fund-raising — Preparation: time limits and deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: All campaign activities should be given a time limit and specific deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fund-raising — Committee work: representative originating group
rubrics_metrics.description: The originating group, whether a committee or a board of directors, should be a representative body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fund-raising — Committee work: strong leadership required
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong leadership is a necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fund-raising — Committee work: individual responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The effectiveness of the group depends on the degree to which individuals accept responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fund-raising — Committee work: committees critique better than create
rubrics_metrics.description: Committees are better at critiquing than creating. Before asking for ideas or suggestions for a plan, give each member of the group a copy of the plan to critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fund-raising — Publicity: sell the idea and the means
rubrics_metrics.description: The first objective of publicity is to sell the idea; the second objective is to sell the means of its accomplishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fund-raising — Publicity: appeal to emotions and intellect
rubrics_metrics.description: Publicity materials should appeal both to the emotions and to the intellect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fund-raising — Publicity: continuity and theme
rubrics_metrics.description: Publicity must have continuity, with all the elements of a campaign tied together with a theme of common appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fund-raising — Publicity: proceed from general to specific
rubrics_metrics.description: Publicity should proceed from the general to the specific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fund-raising — Publicity: general-application appeal generates interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest in an idea proceeds from an appeal of general application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fund-raising — Publicity: quality over cheapness
rubrics_metrics.description: Cheap publicity is expensive. Quality in publicity efforts pays dividends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fund-raising — Publicity: be positive and highlight strengths
rubrics_metrics.description: Publicity should be positive and not negative. Effective publicity always plays up elements of strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fund-raising — Campaign operation: solve immediate needs and build foundation
rubrics_metrics.description: A campaign should solve immediate financial needs and lay a firm foundation for future campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fund-raising — Campaign operation: effective canvassing answers five questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective canvassing answers five questions: why, where, who, what, and how.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fund-raising — Campaign operation: periodic milestones to maintain interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Campaigns should periodically reach milestones to arouse and maintain interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fund-raising — Campaign operation: atmosphere of universality in canvassing
rubrics_metrics.description: All canvassing, even for special gifts, should be conducted in an atmosphere of universality. Prospects typically ask, “What are others doing?”

rubrics_metrics.name: Fund-raising — Campaign operation: steady pressure and urgency
rubrics_metrics.description: Campaigns should be conducted under a steady and constant pressure and sense of urgency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fund-raising — Campaign operation: time spent varies with goal and appeal popularity
rubrics_metrics.description: The time spent on a campaign varies directly with the size of the goal and inversely with the popularity of the appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fund-raising — Campaign operation: direct appeal at peak interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The direct appeal for help should be made when interest is at its peak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fund-raising — Campaign operation: four tests of effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four tests of the effectiveness of campaign operations: quality, quantity, cost, and time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fund-raising — Campaign operation: impact measured by objective achievement
rubrics_metrics.description: Campaign impact is determined by the degree to which the campaign objectives were achieved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern nonprofit PR — integration with marketing and business development
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations is more integrated with marketing and business development in contemporary nonprofit practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern nonprofit PR — leadership engagement of professional PR practitioners
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders in the nonprofit sector (boards, trustees, program managers) are beginning to engage professional public relations practitioners—either hiring staff or outside consultants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern nonprofit PR — standard expectations: recruit volunteers and ensure financial stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Recruiting volunteers, gaining public support, and helping achieve financial stability are standard expectations of the public relations role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tactic — paid advertising as controlled communications
rubrics_metrics.description: Paid advertising has emerged as a major controlled communications tactic for nonprofit organizations, particularly for the health care industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tactic — cause marketing and strategic partnerships
rubrics_metrics.description: Cause marketing and strategic partnerships that link nonprofits with corporate donors and sometimes media organizations are increasingly popular as ways to enhance the reputation of nonprofits and their corporate partners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'On Deck for the Cure' (Susan G. Komen + cruise lines), Neutrogena + American Cancer Society 'Pale is the New Tan' T-shirt partnership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology and social media — speed, capability, ethics, and crisis risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Technology—including Web-based communication, emerging electronic media, and portable communication devices—has increased the speed and capability of communication, but has raised questions about ethics and privacy. Occasionally, the convenience and speed of social media platforms such as Twitter, Facebook, and YouTube create crises for organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the Red Cross 'mistweet' example: prompt, lighthearted, audience-appropriate responses can defuse mistakes and even generate positive outcomes (donations, viral attention).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public relations responsibility — rebuild and maintain public confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations is charged with both helping rebuild credibility and maintaining or trying to restore public confidence in charitable agencies and voluntary groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is especially important given scandals and declining public trust in some nonprofits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embedding journalists — program accomplishments to evaluate
rubrics_metrics.description: Embedding journalists resulted in unprecedented access, better understanding of military life, reporters also serving as the link back home, greater trust that eased some tension, increased information exchange, and better military–media relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also noted: embedding 'humanizes both the journalist responsible for informing the public and the soldier tasked with protecting the people' and provides an empathetic forum and realistic coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professionalization — training and advanced education for military public affairs officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Military public affairs officers have been trained at Defense Information School or university public relations programs; accelerated master's programs and professional development have increased strategic thinking and theoretical foundation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: San Diego State University's accelerated master's program for active duty public affairs officers led officers to be 'more strategic' and better prepared for day-to-day work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional credential — APR+M certification
rubrics_metrics.description: APR+M indicates that the public affairs specialist has met all the qualifications of PRSA accreditation and has completed a rigorous course of study about military public affairs in joint operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: APR+M recognizes the professional status of military public affairs specialists and serves as an accreditation standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration with operations — seat at the management table
rubrics_metrics.description: Public affairs officers participate in command-level meetings (e.g., 'morning standup'), provide public affairs counsel to command leadership about media implications, and are integrated into operational briefings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nearly every kinetic operation brief includes a note on whether a press release was issued; public affairs touches all operations on the battlefield.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience-centered approach — tailor messages and channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Know one’s audience and tailor the approach; while the core information may be the same, the approach should be tailored to each audience (e.g., Afghan TV vs. BBC). Understand how people get their news and information for effective outreach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In low-literacy environments, prioritize television and radio over print; message form and channel selection must match audience media habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational competence — be fully trained and prepared for high-stakes environments
rubrics_metrics.description: Being a public affairs officer at war requires being fully trained and armed with expert knowledge of public affairs; long hours, complex stakeholder environments, and high stakes demand advanced skills to 'break through' barriers and tell difficult stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work includes management/environmental scanning, briefing commanders, fielding media queries, and strategic message planning.
